claim: EphB4 is expressed in veins, venules and small capillaries in the adult heart ventricle.
source: EphB4 is expressed in veins, venules (white arrowheads) and small capillaries (blue arrowheads) in the adult heart ventricle.
evidence: Immunohistochemistry images in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A show EphB4 expression pattern in cardiac vessels.

claim: Ephrin-B2 is expressed in small capillaries of the ventricular wall and in arteries.
source: Concomitant expression of GFP shows that ephrin-B2 is expressed in the small capillaries of the ventricular wall (arrowheads) and in arteries.
evidence: Immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B demonstrates ephrin-B2 expression using GFP reporter.

claim: Cdh5CreERT2 R26-mTmG mice show GFP expression throughout the cardiac endothelium at 4 weeks after tamoxifen induction.
source: Cdh5CreERT2 R26-mTmG double heterozygous mice show GFP expression throughout the cardiac endothelium at 4 weeks after tamoxifen induction.
evidence: Figure 1—figure supplement 1C shows high recombination efficiency in cardiac ECs.

claim: EphB4 protein expression is abolished in Ephb4∆EC cardiac veins, venules and capillaries.
source: EphB4 protein expression is abolished in Ephb4∆EC cardiac veins, venules (white arrowheads) and capillaries (blue arrowheads).
evidence: Immunohistochemistry in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D demonstrates loss of EphB4 expression in mutant vessels.

claim: Western blot analysis confirms strongly reduced EphB4 expression in Ephb4∆EC mutants at 12 weeks.
source: Western blot analysis of total heart lysate at 12 weeks confirms strongly reduced EphB4 expression in Ephb4∆EC mutants.
evidence: Figure 1—figure supplement 1E shows Western blot data demonstrating reduced EphB4 protein levels.

claim: Ephb4∆EC mutant hearts weigh 20% more than controls on average.
source: On average, mutant hearts weighed 20% more than controls, whereas total body weight was not significantly altered.
evidence: Morphometric data presented in Figure 1A shows increased heart weight in mutants.

claim: Heart weight normalized to tibia length is increased in Ephb4∆EC mutants.
source: Normalization of heart weight to tibia length (Yin et al., 1982) confirmed this finding (Figure 1A).
evidence: Figure 1A shows quantification of heart weight/tibia length ratio.

claim: Cardiomyocytes are significantly enlarged in Ephb4∆EC hearts.
source: Histologic analysis of the left ventricle's cardiac wall revealed a significant enlargement of the cardiomyocytes in Ephb4∆EC hearts (Figure 1B), indicating hypertrophic remodeling of the heart muscle.
evidence: Figure 1B shows immunohistochemistry data with quantification of cardiomyocyte relative area.

claim: Ephb4∆EC mutant hearts show reduced ejection fraction.
source: Moreover, echocardiography analysis of mutant hearts showed a reduced heart ejection fraction and larger left ventricle diastolic and systolic volumes (Figure 1C and Figure 1—videos 1 and 2).
evidence: Echocardiography data in Figure 1C demonstrates functional cardiac defects.

claim: Ephb4∆EC mutant hearts have larger left ventricle diastolic and systolic volumes.
source: Moreover, echocardiography analysis of mutant hearts showed a reduced heart ejection fraction and larger left ventricle diastolic and systolic volumes (Figure 1C and Figure 1—videos 1 and 2).
evidence: Echocardiography measurements shown in Figure 1C quantify ventricular volumes.

claim: The interventricular septum walls are significantly thinner in Ephb4∆EC mutants.
source: Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging (CMRI) revealed that the walls of the organ were significantly thinner at the interventricular septum and that the mass of the left ventricle was lower, whereas the right ventricle was not affected at this stage (Figure 1D and Figure 1—videos 3–6).
evidence: CMRI data in Figure 1D shows measurements of ventricular septum thickness.

claim: The mass of the left ventricle is lower in Ephb4∆EC mutants.
source: Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging (CMRI) revealed that the walls of the organ were significantly thinner at the interventricular septum and that the mass of the left ventricle was lower, whereas the right ventricle was not affected at this stage (Figure 1D and Figure 1—videos 3–6).
evidence: CMRI analysis in Figure 1D quantifies left ventricular mass.

claim: The right ventricle is not affected in Ephb4∆EC mutants at 12 weeks.
source: Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging (CMRI) revealed that the walls of the organ were significantly thinner at the interventricular septum and that the mass of the left ventricle was lower, whereas the right ventricle was not affected at this stage (Figure 1D and Figure 1—videos 3–6).
evidence: CMRI data in Figure 1D shows no significant change in right ventricular mass.

claim: Ephb4∆EC mutant ventricles undergo ongoing dilation.
source: These observations indicate ongoing dilation of Ephb4∆EC mutant ventricles.
evidence: Inference based on CMRI and echocardiography data showing ventricular changes.

claim: Ephb4∆EC mutant mice have reduced vascular density with less coronary vessel branch points.
source: Interestingly, histologic analysis revealed that mutant mice have reduced vascular density with less coronary vessel branch points (Figure 2A), an effect that could be partially influenced by the increased cardiomyocyte area.
evidence: Figure 2A shows immunostaining data with quantification of branching points.

claim: There is a significant loss of mural cell coverage in blood vessels of the Ephb4∆EC ventricle.
source: In addition, immunostaining against PDGFRβ, a marker of pericytes and vascular smooth muscle cells associated with the endothelial monolayer, showed a significant loss of mural cell coverage in the blood vessels of the ventricle, which was especially prominent in certain capillaries (Figure 2B).
evidence: Figure 2B shows immunostaining data with quantification of pericyte coverage.

claim: Extravasated erythrocytes were detected in the Ephb4∆EC myocardium, indicating microhemorrhages.
source: Moreover, extravasated erythrocytes were detected in the mutant myocardium, indicating the presence of microhemorrhages in the Ephb4∆EC ventricular wall (Figure 2C).
evidence: Figure 2C shows immunostaining revealing erythrocytes outside vessels.

claim: Mutant ECs do not show increased cell death as indicated by comparable TUNEL staining.
source: Nevertheless, mutant ECs did not show increased cell death, as indicated by comparable TUNEL staining in control and mutant ventricles (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: TUNEL assay data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A shows no detectable cell death in mutant ECs.

claim: Pimonidazole administration did not indicate appreciable tissue hypoxia in Ephb4∆EC hearts.
source: Analysis of tissue oxygenation through Pimonidazole administration did not indicate appreciable tissue hypoxia, arguing for sufficient oxygen transport through the Ephb4∆EC endothelium (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B,C).
evidence: Hypoxia assay data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B,C shows no hypoxia signal in mutant hearts.

claim: Loss of EphB4 in ECs did not induce fibrosis in the mutant myocardium.
source: It is also noteworthy that loss of EphB4 in ECs did not induce fibrosis in the mutant myocardium (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A,B).
evidence: Collagen staining and Masson's Gold Trichrome staining in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A,B show no fibrosis.

claim: Mutant endothelial cells are irregularly arranged and display an expanded cytoplasm largely devoid of vesicles.
source: High magnification images revealed that mutant ECs were irregularly arranged and displayed an expanded cytoplasm largely devoid of vesicles, whereas caveolar structures were abundant along the basolateral membrane (Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 3A–C).
evidence: TEM images in Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 3A show ultrastructural changes in mutant ECs.

claim: Caveolar structures are abundant along the basolateral membrane of mutant ECs.
source: High magnification images revealed that mutant ECs were irregularly arranged and displayed an expanded cytoplasm largely devoid of vesicles, whereas caveolar structures were abundant along the basolateral membrane (Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 3A–C).
evidence: TEM images in Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 3B,C show accumulation of caveolae at the basolateral membrane.

claim: Mutant cardiomyocytes show accumulation of glycogen granules in their cytoplasm close to mitochondria.
source: Moreover, mutant cardiomyocytes showed the accumulation of glycogen granules in their cytoplasm close to the mitochondria (Figure 2—figure supplement 3D).
evidence: TEM images in Figure 2—figure supplement 3D show glycogen accumulation near mitochondria.

claim: Transport through the endothelium and cardiomyocyte metabolism might be affected in Ephb4∆EC mutant hearts.
source: These observations suggest that the transport through the endothelium and cardiomyocyte metabolism might be affected in Ephb4∆EC mutant hearts.
evidence: Inference based on TEM observations of caveolar accumulation and glycogen deposits.

claim: TEM revealed ruptures of the capillaries in Ephb4∆EC hearts.
source: TEM also revealed ruptures of the capillaries explaining the microhemorrhages mentioned above (Figure 2D).
evidence: TEM images in Figure 2D show vascular ruptures with thrombocytes.

claim: The phenotype observed upon EC-specific loss of ephrin-B2 was milder than the defects in Ephb4∆EC hearts.
source: The phenotype observed upon EC-specific loss of ephrin-B2 was milder than the defects in Ephb4∆EC hearts.
evidence: Comparison of phenotypes between Efnb2∆EC and Ephb4∆EC mutants described in text and shown in Figure 3.

claim: Efnb2∆EC heart weight was not altered at 12 weeks.
source: While Efnb2∆EC heart weight was not altered (Figure 3A), the cardiomyocyte relative area was significantly increased (Figure 3B).
evidence: Figure 3A shows heart weight measurements for Efnb2∆EC mutants.

claim: Cardiomyocyte relative area was significantly increased in Efnb2∆EC hearts at 12 weeks.
source: While Efnb2∆EC heart weight was not altered (Figure 3A), the cardiomyocyte relative area was significantly increased (Figure 3B).
evidence: Figure 3B shows immunohistochemistry data with quantification of cardiomyocyte area.

claim: Vascular density was not appreciably altered in Efnb2∆EC hearts at 12 weeks.
source: Vascular density (Figure 3C) and perivascular coverage of the capillaries (Figure 3D) was not appreciably altered.
evidence: Figure 3C shows quantification of branching points in Efnb2∆EC hearts.

claim: Perivascular coverage of capillaries was not appreciably altered in Efnb2∆EC hearts at 12 weeks.
source: Vascular density (Figure 3C) and perivascular coverage of the capillaries (Figure 3D) was not appreciably altered.
evidence: Figure 3D shows immunostaining data with quantification of pericyte coverage.

claim: Ephb4∆EC hearts at 10 weeks did not show a significant weight increase.
source: Ephb4∆EC hearts at this stage did not show yet a significant weight increase (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A) but their cardiomyocytes were already hypertrophic, resulting in a significant increase in relative area (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Figure 3—figure supplement 1A shows heart weight data at 10 weeks.

claim: Cardiomyocytes in Ephb4∆EC hearts at 10 weeks were already hypertrophic.
source: Ephb4∆EC hearts at this stage did not show yet a significant weight increase (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A) but their cardiomyocytes were already hypertrophic, resulting in a significant increase in relative area (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Figure 3—figure supplement 1B shows cardiomyocyte relative area measurements at 10 weeks.

claim: Both Efnb2∆EC hearts at 12 weeks and Ephb4∆EC hearts at 10 weeks presented microhemorrhages.
source: Both, Efnb2∆EC hearts at 12 weeks and Ephb4∆EC hearts at 10 weeks hearts presented microhemorrhages (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A,B).
evidence: Figure 3—figure supplement 2A,B shows immunostaining revealing erythrocytes outside vessels.

claim: Skeletal muscle was unaffected after EC-specific inactivation of Ephb4.
source: In contrast to the defects seen in cardiac muscle, skeletal muscle was unaffected after the EC-specific inactivation of Ephb4.
evidence: Analysis of skeletal muscle shown in Figure 4B-D demonstrates no significant changes.

claim: Vascular density in skeletal muscle remained unchanged in Ephb4∆EC mutants.
source: Both vascular density (Figure 4B) and pericyte coverage (Figure 4C) of capillaries remained unchanged and, most importantly, the relative area occupied by myocytes was not significantly altered (Figure 4D).
evidence: Figure 4B shows quantification of branching points in skeletal muscle.

claim: Pericyte coverage of capillaries in skeletal muscle remained unchanged in Ephb4∆EC mutants.
source: Both vascular density (Figure 4B) and pericyte coverage (Figure 4C) of capillaries remained unchanged and, most importantly, the relative area occupied by myocytes was not significantly altered (Figure 4D).
evidence: Figure 4C shows quantification of pericyte coverage in skeletal muscle.

claim: The relative area occupied by myocytes in skeletal muscle was not significantly altered in Ephb4∆EC mutants.
source: Both vascular density (Figure 4B) and pericyte coverage (Figure 4C) of capillaries remained unchanged and, most importantly, the relative area occupied by myocytes was not significantly altered (Figure 4D).
evidence: Figure 4D shows quantification of myocyte relative area in skeletal muscle.

claim: The vasculature of kidney and liver was not appreciably altered in Ephb4∆EC mutants.
source: Likewise, the vasculature of other organs, namely kidney and liver, was not appreciably altered in EphB4∆EC mutants (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: Figure 4—figure supplement 1A-C shows immunostaining of kidney and liver vasculature.

claim: Heart size and cardiomyocyte relative area remained unaffected in Ephb4∆LEC mutants.
source: Despite efficient EphB4 deletion in lymphatic vessels (Ephb4∆LEC) after 4-hydroxy tamoxifen administration (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A), heart size and cardiomyocyte relative area remained unaffected (Figure 4—figure supplement 2B,C).
evidence: Figure 4—figure supplement 2B,C shows heart weight and cardiomyocyte measurements in Ephb4∆LEC mutants.

claim: The heart phenotype arises due to loss of EphB4 in blood vessels but not the lymphatic vasculature.
source: These results argue that the heart phenotype arises due to loss of EphB4 in blood vessels but not the lymphatic vasculature.
evidence: Comparison of Ephb4∆EC and Ephb4∆LEC phenotypes demonstrates blood vessel-specific requirement.

claim: Differential gene expression analysis identified 529 genes (p<0.05) of which 268 were upregulated and 261 downregulated in Ephb4∆EC ventricles.
source: Differential gene expression analysis identified 529 genes (p<0.05) of which 268 were upregulated and 261 downregulated (Figure 5A; Figure 5—figure supplement 1A and Figure 5—source data 1).
evidence: RNA-seq data shown in Figure 5A demonstrates differentially expressed genes.

claim: Genes related to coronary artery disease, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and dilated cardiomyopathy were dysregulated in Ephb4∆EC hearts.
source: First, the analysis revealed that genes related to human disease, and in particular to coronary artery disease, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM) and DCM were dysregulated in Ephb4∆EC hearts (Figure 5B).
evidence: Gene ontology analysis in Figure 5B shows enrichment of disease-related genes.

claim: Genes related to regulation of carbohydrate metabolism and positive regulation of glycolysis were upregulated in Ephb4∆EC samples.
source: Further GO analysis of biological processes revealed that genes related to the regulation of carbohydrate metabolism and the positive regulation of glycolysis were upregulated in mutant samples.
evidence: Gene ontology analysis shown in Figure 5C demonstrates upregulation of metabolic genes.

claim: Glucose consumption and glycolysis in the heart are indicators of cardiomyopathy.
source: These observations are interesting because glucose consumption and glycolysis in the heart are indicators of cardiomyopathy (Ritterhoff and Tian, 2017) (Figure 5C and Figure 5—source data 1).
evidence: Citation to Ritterhoff and Tian, 2017 provides established knowledge about cardiac metabolism in disease.

claim: Genes related to extracellular matrix organization were downregulated in Ephb4∆EC hearts.
source: We also observed that genes related to extracellular matrix (ECM) organization were downregulated in Ephb4∆EC hearts (Figure 5D and Figure 5—source data 1).
evidence: Gene ontology analysis in Figure 5D shows downregulation of ECM-related genes.

claim: FoxO signaling pathway genes (Agap2, Pten, Igf1, Pik3r1, Foxo3 and Pck2) were upregulated in Ephb4∆EC hearts.
source: In particular, two signaling pathways strongly related to cardiac metabolism and disease were altered: FoxO signaling and the genes Agap2, Pten, Igf1, Pik3r1, Foxo3 and Pck2 were upregulated, whereas mTOR signaling and the genes Irs1, Rragd, Hif1a and Vegfa were downregulated in mutant hearts (Figure 5E,F; Figure 5—figure supplement 1B,C and Figure 5—source data 1) (Ronnebaum and Patterson, 2010; Schips et al., 2011; Sciarretta et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2010).
evidence: KEGG pathway analysis in Figure 5E and gene expression data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B show upregulated genes.

claim: mTOR signaling pathway genes (Irs1, Rragd, Hif1a and Vegfa) were downregulated in Ephb4∆EC hearts.
source: In particular, two signaling pathways strongly related to cardiac metabolism and disease were altered: FoxO signaling and the genes Agap2, Pten, Igf1, Pik3r1, Foxo3 and Pck2 were upregulated, whereas mTOR signaling and the genes Irs1, Rragd, Hif1a and Vegfa were downregulated in mutant hearts (Figure 5E,F; Figure 5—figure supplement 1B,C and Figure 5—source data 1) (Ronnebaum and Patterson, 2010; Schips et al., 2011; Sciarretta et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2010).
evidence: KEGG pathway analysis in Figure 5F and gene expression data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C show downregulated genes.

claim: Mass spectrometry revealed 455 significantly altered proteins (p<0.05), of which 206 were upregulated and 249 downregulated in Ephb4∆EC ventricles.
source: This revealed a total of 455 significant altered proteins (p<0.05), of which 206 were upregulated and 249 downregulated (Figure 5—figure supplement 1E and Figure 5—source data 2).
evidence: Mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1E demonstrates protein-level changes.

claim: GO analysis revealed upregulation of metabolic processes in Ephb4∆EC ventricles.
source: Remarkably, GO analysis of biological processes in the mutant ventricles revealed an upregulation of metabolic processes (Figure 5—figure supplement 1F) accompanied by downregulation of endocytic recycling (Figure 5—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: Gene ontology analysis of proteomics data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1F shows upregulated processes.

claim: GO analysis revealed downregulation of endocytic recycling in Ephb4∆EC ventricles.
source: Remarkably, GO analysis of biological processes in the mutant ventricles revealed an upregulation of metabolic processes (Figure 5—figure supplement 1F) accompanied by downregulation of endocytic recycling (Figure 5—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: Gene ontology analysis of proteomics data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1G shows downregulated processes.

claim: Cardiac remodeling in Ephb4∆EC mutants is linked to defective transport processes and a metabolic shift towards glycolysis in heart.
source: Altogether these results suggest that cardiac remodeling in Ephb4∆EC mutants is linked to defective transport processes and a metabolic shift towards glycolysis in heart.
evidence: Inference based on combined RNA-seq and proteomics data showing metabolic and transport changes.

claim: Stimulation with recombinant ephrin-B2/Fc protein induces phosphorylation of Akt in HUVECs.
source: In cultured human umbilical vein endothelial cells (HUVECs), stimulation with recombinant and soluble ephrin-B2/Fc protein induces phosphorylation of Akt and Src, which is blocked by the pathway-specific inhibitors LY294002 and PP2, respectively (Figure 6A,B).
evidence: Western blot data in Figure 6A,B shows increased pAkt after ephrin-B2/Fc treatment.

claim: Stimulation with recombinant ephrin-B2/Fc protein induces phosphorylation of Src in HUVECs.
source: In cultured human umbilical vein endothelial cells (HUVECs), stimulation with recombinant and soluble ephrin-B2/Fc protein induces phosphorylation of Akt and Src, which is blocked by the pathway-specific inhibitors LY294002 and PP2, respectively (Figure 6A,B).
evidence: Western blot data in Figure 6A,B shows increased pSrc after ephrin-B2/Fc treatment.

claim: LY294002 blocks ephrin-B2/Fc-induced phosphorylation of Akt in HUVECs.
source: In cultured human umbilical vein endothelial cells (HUVECs), stimulation with recombinant and soluble ephrin-B2/Fc protein induces phosphorylation of Akt and Src, which is blocked by the pathway-specific inhibitors LY294002 and PP2, respectively (Figure 6A,B).
evidence: Western blot data in Figure 6A,B shows LY294002 inhibits Akt phosphorylation.

claim: PP2 blocks ephrin-B2/Fc-induced phosphorylation of Src in HUVECs.
source: In cultured human umbilical vein endothelial cells (HUVECs), stimulation with recombinant and soluble ephrin-B2/Fc protein induces phosphorylation of Akt and Src, which is blocked by the pathway-specific inhibitors LY294002 and PP2, respectively (Figure 6A,B).
evidence: Western blot data in Figure 6A,B shows PP2 inhibits Src phosphorylation.

claim: Levels of phosphorylated ERK1/2 were reduced after ephrin-B2/Fc treatment in HUVECs.
source: In contrast, levels of phosphorylated ERK1/2 were reduced after ephrin-B2/Fc treatment.
evidence: Western blot data in Figure 6A,B shows decreased pERK1/2 after ephrin-B2/Fc treatment.

claim: Stimulation with EphB4/Fc led to activation of Src but not of Akt and ERK1/2 in cultured HUVECs.
source: Stimulation with EphB4/Fc, which is known to activate signaling through the cytoplasmic domain of ephrin-B2 (Palmer et al., 2002), led to activation of Src but not of Akt and ERK1/2 in cultured HUVECs (Figure 6A,B).
evidence: Western blot data in Figure 6A,B shows selective Src activation by EphB4/Fc.

claim: There is overlap between EphB4 receptor and phosphorylated caveolin 1 (CAV1) in HUVECs.
source: We also noted overlap between EphB4 receptor, detected by binding of ephrin-B2/Fc, and phosphorylated caveolin 1 (CAV1) (Figure 6C), an integral membrane protein in caveolar membranes and regulator of caveolae-mediated endocytosis.
evidence: Immunostaining in Figure 6C shows colocalization of EphB4 and pCAV1.

claim: Phosphorylation of caveolin has been linked to Src kinase.
source: Interestingly, previous work has linked phosphorylation of caveolin to Src kinase (Li et al., 1996; Sverdlov et al., 2007).
evidence: Citations to Li et al., 1996 and Sverdlov et al., 2007 provide established knowledge.

claim: Transfection of siEPHB4 efficiently abolished expression of EphB4 at protein level in HUVECs.
source: Transfection of siEPHB4 efficiently abolished expression of the receptor tyrosine kinase at protein level, as assessed by Western blotting (Figure 7A,C).
evidence: Western blot data in Figure 7A,C shows loss of EphB4 protein after siRNA treatment.

claim: Knockdown of EPHB4 resulted in significant reductions of phospho-Src in HUVECs.
source: Knockdown of EPHB4 also resulted in significant reductions of phospho-Src and phosphorylated CAV1, the latter of which was also profoundly reduced in HUVECs treated with siCAV1 siRNA (Figure 7A–C).
evidence: Western blot data in Figure 7A-C shows reduced pSrc after EPHB4 knockdown.

claim: Knockdown of EPHB4 resulted in significant reductions of phosphorylated CAV1 in HUVECs.
source: Knockdown of EPHB4 also resulted in significant reductions of phospho-Src and phosphorylated CAV1, the latter of which was also profoundly reduced in HUVECs treated with siCAV1 siRNA (Figure 7A–C).
evidence: Western blot data in Figure 7A-C shows reduced pCAV1 after EPHB4 knockdown.

claim: CAV1 and phospho-CAV1 were significantly reduced after knockdown of EPHB4 or CAV1 in HUVECs.
source: CAV1 and phospho-CAV1 immunostaining decorate the cytoplasm and the Golgi apparatus, identified by anti-GM130 antibody signal, and both CAV1 and phospho-CAV1 were significantly reduced after knockdown of EPHB4 or CAV1 (Figure 7D,E).
evidence: Immunostaining data in Figure 7D,E shows reduced CAV1 and pCAV1 signals after knockdown.

claim: siEPHB4 or siCAV1 transfection of HUVECs led to a significant increase in cell size.
source: siEPHB4 or siCAV1 transfection of HUVECs also led to a significant increase in cell size (Figure 8—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Cell area quantification in Figure 8—figure supplement 1A shows increased cell size.

claim: Ephrin-B2/Fc treatment of HUVECs significantly increased phospho-CAV1.
source: Further arguing for EphB4-induced phosphorylation of CAV1 through Src, ephrin-B2/Fc treatment of HUVECs significantly increased phospho-CAV1, which was blocked by addition of the Src family kinase inhibitor PP2 (Figure 8A,B).
evidence: Western blot data in Figure 8A,B shows increased pCAV1 after ephrin-B2/Fc treatment.

claim: PP2 blocked ephrin-B2/Fc-induced increase in phospho-CAV1 in HUVECs.
source: Further arguing for EphB4-induced phosphorylation of CAV1 through Src, ephrin-B2/Fc treatment of HUVECs significantly increased phospho-CAV1, which was blocked by addition of the Src family kinase inhibitor PP2 (Figure 8A,B).
evidence: Western blot data in Figure 8A,B shows PP2 blocks pCAV1 increase.

claim: EphB4/Fc treatment did not lead to appreciable changes in phospho-CAV1 in HUVECs.
source: In contrast, EphB4/Fc treatment did not lead to appreciable changes in phospho-CAV1 (Figure 8A,B).
evidence: Western blot data in Figure 8A,B shows no change in pCAV1 after EphB4/Fc treatment.

claim: Stimulation with ephrin-B2/Fc increased phospho-CAV1 signals in HUVECs, which was blocked by PP2.
source: In immunostainings, stimulation with ephrin-B2/Fc increased phospho-CAV1 signals, which was blocked by presence of PP2 (Figure 8C–E).
evidence: Immunostaining data in Figure 8C-E shows increased pCAV1 signal and PP2 inhibition.

claim: Inhibition of PI3K-Akt with LY294002 or of MAPK/ERK with U0126 had no significant effect on CAV1 phosphorylation.
source: In contrast, inhibition of PI3K-Akt with LY294002 or of MAPK/ERK with U0126 had no significant effect on CAV1 phosphorylation (Figure 8D,E and Figure 8—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Data in Figure 8D,E and Figure 8—figure supplement 1C shows no effect of LY294002 or U0126 on pCAV1.

claim: The increase in CAV1 phosphorylation after ephrin-B2 stimulation was suppressed in HUVECs treated with siEPHB4.
source: Confirming that the effect of ephrin-B2/Fc is indeed mediated by EphB4 and not another member of the large Eph receptor family, the increase in CAV1 phosphorylation after ephrin-B2 stimulation was suppressed in HUVECs treated with siEPHB4 (Figure 8G).
evidence: Western blot data in Figure 8G shows siEPHB4 blocks ephrin-B2-induced pCAV1 increase.

claim: EphB4 activation triggers the phosphorylation of CAV1 through the cytoplasmic kinase Src.
source: Together, these results argue that EphB4 activation triggers the phosphorylation of CAV1 through the cytoplasmic kinase Src, which generates a molecular link to caveolar transport in ECs and provides an explanation for the observed accumulation of caveolae at the basolateral membrane of the Ephb4∆EC cardiac endothelium.
evidence: Inference based on combined data from Fc stimulation, inhibitor treatments, and knockdown experiments.

claim: Flow cytometry revealed significant reductions in the uptake of albumin upon EphB4 downregulation in HUVECs.
source: Flow cytometry and the analysis of stained cells revealed significant reductions in the uptake of albumin, a caveolae-dependent process, upon EphB4 downregulation (Figure 9A,C and Figure 9—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: Flow cytometry data in Figure 9A,C and Figure 9—figure supplement 1A,B shows reduced BSA uptake.

claim: Transfection with siCAV1 impaired the uptake of albumin in HUVECs.
source: Similarly, transfection with siCAV1 impaired the uptake of albumin (Figure 9A,C).
evidence: Immunostaining and quantification in Figure 9A,C shows reduced BSA uptake after siCAV1.

claim: The clathrin-controlled uptake of transferrin was unaffected in non-permeabilized siEPHB4 cells.
source: In contrast, the clathrin-controlled uptake of transferrin was unaffected in non-permeabilized siEPHB4 cells and slightly reduced after permeabilization and immunostaining (Figure 9—figure supplement 1C–F).
evidence: Flow cytometry data in Figure 9—figure supplement 1C shows no change in transferrin uptake.

claim: EphB4 downregulation resulted in significantly reduced fatty acid uptake in HUVECs.
source: This approach revealed significantly reduced fatty acid uptake in siEPHB4 HUVECs relative to control cells, based on both flow cytometry data and the analysis of stained cells (Figure 9B,C and Figure 9—figure supplement 1G,H).
evidence: BODIPY uptake data in Figure 9B,C and Figure 9—figure supplement 1G,H shows reduced fatty acid uptake.

claim: CD36 is a membrane receptor mediating the endocytosis of fatty acids and requires caveolar transport for its correct localization and function.
source: CD36 is a membrane receptor mediating the endocytosis of fatty acids and requires caveolar transport for its correct localization and function (Ring et al., 2006).
evidence: Citation to Ring et al., 2006 provides established knowledge about CD36 function.

claim: Surface CD36 was significantly reduced in siEPHB4 and siCAV1 transfected HUVECs relative to control cells.
source: While immunostaining of siEPHB4 and siCAV1 transfected HUVECs revealed no change in total CD36 immunosignal relative to control cells (Figure 7E and Figure 7—figure supplement 1A), surface CD36 was significantly reduced relative to control cells (Figure 7D,E).
evidence: Immunostaining data in Figure 7D,E shows reduced surface CD36 after knockdown.

claim: CD36 localization to Golgi was increased after knockdown of EPHB4 or CAV1 in HUVECs.
source: Further, CD36 localization to Golgi was increased after knockdown of EPHB4 or CAV1 (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A,B), potentially indicating CD36 synthesis and thereby a compensatory response to reduced fatty acid uptake.
evidence: Immunostaining data in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A,B shows increased Golgi-localized CD36.

claim: CD36 immunosignal is downregulated in capillaries of the Ephb4∆EC myocardium.
source: In vivo, CD36 immunosignal is downregulated in capillaries of the Ephb4∆EC myocardium but appears upregulated in the membrane of cardiomyocytes, again suggesting a potential compensatory mechanism to restore fatty acid uptake (Figure 9D).
evidence: Immunostaining in Figure 9D shows reduced CD36 in mutant capillaries.

claim: CD36 appears upregulated in the membrane of cardiomyocytes in Ephb4∆EC hearts.
source: In vivo, CD36 immunosignal is downregulated in capillaries of the Ephb4∆EC myocardium but appears upregulated in the membrane of cardiomyocytes, again suggesting a potential compensatory mechanism to restore fatty acid uptake (Figure 9D).
evidence: Immunostaining in Figure 9D shows increased CD36 in cardiomyocyte membranes.

claim: Glucose concentration was reduced in Ephb4∆EC mutant plasma relative to littermate controls.
source: Glucose concentration was reduced in mutant plasma relative to littermate controls, whereas levels of triglycerides and free fatty acids appeared unaffected (Figure 9—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: Plasma analysis data in Figure 9—figure supplement 2A shows reduced glucose levels.

claim: Levels of triglycerides and free fatty acids in plasma appeared unaffected in Ephb4∆EC mutants.
source: Glucose concentration was reduced in mutant plasma relative to littermate controls, whereas levels of triglycerides and free fatty acids appeared unaffected (Figure 9—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: Plasma analysis data in Figure 9—figure supplement 2A shows no change in triglycerides and free fatty acids.

claim: Histological analysis of Ephb4∆EC livers revealed the accumulation of fat.
source: Interestingly, histological analysis of Ephb4∆EC livers revealed the accumulation of fat (Figure 9—figure supplement 2B), suggesting that defective caveolar transport and fatty acid uptake by mutant cardiac ECs is accompanied by ectopic lipid deposition in liver.
evidence: Oil Red O staining in Figure 9—figure supplement 2B shows fat accumulation in liver.

claim: Defective caveolar transport and fatty acid uptake by mutant cardiac ECs is accompanied by ectopic lipid deposition in liver.
source: Interestingly, histological analysis of Ephb4∆EC livers revealed the accumulation of fat (Figure 9—figure supplement 2B), suggesting that defective caveolar transport and fatty acid uptake by mutant cardiac ECs is accompanied by ectopic lipid deposition in liver.
evidence: Inference based on liver fat accumulation and cardiac fatty acid uptake defects.

claim: siEPHB4 transfection reduced the accumulation and localization of focal adhesion proteins in cell junctions under static conditions in HUVECs.
source: In cultured HUVECs, siEPHB4 transfection reduced the accumulation and localization of focal adhesion proteins in cell junctions under static conditions, whereas VE-Cadherin localization was maintained (Figure 10A,C).
evidence: Immunostaining data in Figure 10A,C shows reduced Vinculin/CDH5 colocalization.

claim: VE-Cadherin localization was maintained in siEPHB4 transfected HUVECs under static conditions.
source: In cultured HUVECs, siEPHB4 transfection reduced the accumulation and localization of focal adhesion proteins in cell junctions under static conditions, whereas VE-Cadherin localization was maintained (Figure 10A,C).
evidence: Immunostaining data in Figure 10A shows maintained VE-Cadherin localization.

claim: Control HUVECs were able to maintain a continuous monolayer under cyclic tension, but siEPHB4 cells were frequently separated by large gaps.
source: When HUVECs were cultured under cyclic tension mimicking 10% of sinusoidal stretch for 24 hr, control cells were able to maintain a continuous monolayer but siEPHB4 cells were frequently separated by large gaps (Figure 10B,C).
evidence: Stretching assay data in Figure 10B,C shows disrupted monolayer in siEPHB4 cells.

claim: Downregulation of EPHB4 results in decreased cell stiffness in HUVECs as indicated by a significant reduction in the Young's Module.
source: Furthermore, atomic force microscopy (AFM) revealed that the downregulation of EPHB4 results in decreased cell stiffness relative to control HUVECs, as indicated by a significant reduction in the Young's Module that measures membrane displacement upon force application with a cantilever (Figure 10D).
evidence: AFM data in Figure 10D shows reduced Young's modulus in siEPHB4 cells.

claim: EphB4 receptor is required for the structural integrity of cultured ECs.
source: Altogether, these results show that the EphB4 receptor is required for the structural integrity of cultured ECs, which may well explain the vessel wall ruptures observed in vivo.
evidence: Inference based on stretching assay and AFM data showing mechanical defects in siEPHB4 cells.

claim: Loss of EphB4 impairs the mechanical properties and transport function of ECs.
source: In conclusion, our results show the loss of EphB4 impairs the mechanical properties and transport function of ECs, which results in capillary ruptures, metabolic alterations, cardiomyocyte hypertrophic remodeling, and heart dilation.
evidence: Summary inference based on all experimental data presented in the study.

claim: Blood vessels acquire organ-specific specialization.
source: There is increasing evidence that blood vessels acquire organ-specific specialization (Augustin and Koh, 2017), which is necessary to deal with specific metabolic needs and other, typically local properties of the surrounding tissue.
evidence: Citation to Augustin and Koh, 2017 provides established knowledge about vascular specialization.

claim: Ephrin-B2 and EphB4 are frequently used as markers for arteries and veins, respectively.
source: While ephrin-B2 and EphB4 are frequently used as markers for arteries and veins, respectively, both molecules are also co-expressed, albeit at lower levels, in cardiac capillaries.
evidence: Established knowledge about ephrin-B2 and EphB4 expression patterns.

claim: Ephrin-B2 and EphB4 are co-expressed, albeit at lower levels, in cardiac capillaries.
source: While ephrin-B2 and EphB4 are frequently used as markers for arteries and veins, respectively, both molecules are also co-expressed, albeit at lower levels, in cardiac capillaries.
evidence: Immunostaining data from Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,B supports this claim.

claim: EC-specific inactivation of the Ephb4 gene induces a hypertrophic response in cardiomyocytes.
source: In line with the close proximity of capillaries and cardiomyocytes, EC-specific inactivation of the Ephb4 gene induces a hypertrophic response in the latter, which triggers heart remodeling and gives rise to a phenotype that resembles human dilated cardiomyopathy in its features and development.
evidence: Data from Figure 1B showing increased cardiomyocyte area supports this claim.

claim: The phenotype of Ephb4∆EC hearts resembles human dilated cardiomyopathy in its features and development.
source: In line with the close proximity of capillaries and cardiomyocytes, EC-specific inactivation of the Ephb4 gene induces a hypertrophic response in the latter, which triggers heart remodeling and gives rise to a phenotype that resembles human dilated cardiomyopathy in its features and development.
evidence: Multiple data points including heart weight, ejection fraction, and ventricular volumes support this comparison.

claim: Oxygen transport to the heart is not appreciably compromised in Ephb4∆EC mutants despite vascular ruptures and microhemorrhaging.
source: While EphB4 signaling is required for nutrient transport and the structural integrity of coronary capillaries, it is noteworthy that oxygen transport to the heart is not appreciably compromised despite vascular ruptures and microhemorrhaging.
evidence: Pimonidazole data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B,C shows no hypoxia.

claim: Defects in the Ephb4-deficient endothelium are linked to compromised caveolar function and reduced CAV1 phosphorylation.
source: At the molecular level, defects in the Ephb4-deficient endothelium are linked to compromised caveolar function and reduced CAV1 phosphorylation, which involves the kinase Src, a known mediator of Eph receptor signaling (Liang et al., 2019; Lisabeth et al., 2013).
evidence: Data from Figures 7 and 8 showing reduced pCAV1 and Src involvement supports this claim.

claim: Stimulated EphB4 associates with CAV1 and induces its phosphorylation at Tyr-14.
source: This is also consistent with a previous report showing that stimulated EphB4 associates with CAV1 and induces its phosphorylation at Tyr-14 (Muto et al., 2011).
evidence: Citation to Muto et al., 2011 provides supporting evidence from prior work.

claim: Src-dependent phosphorylation of Tyr-14 in CAV1 promotes swelling of caveolae and their release from the plasma membrane.
source: Src-dependent phosphorylation of this residue in CAV1 promotes swelling of caveolae and their release from the plasma membrane (Zimnicka et al., 2016).
evidence: Citation to Zimnicka et al., 2016 provides established knowledge about CAV1 phosphorylation function.

claim: CAV1 has been shown to be required for signaling by EphB1.
source: CAV1 has also been shown to be required for signaling by EphB1, a receptor that is closely related to EphB4 (Vihanto, 2006).
evidence: Citation to Vihanto, 2006 provides supporting evidence from prior work.

claim: CAV1 has been reported to be cardioprotective.
source: CAV1 has been reported to be cardioprotective (Das et al., 2012) and its absence is associated with cardiac hypertrophy (Cohen et al., 2003).
evidence: Citations to Das et al., 2012 and Cohen et al., 2003 provide established knowledge.

claim: Absence of CAV1 is associated with cardiac hypertrophy.
source: CAV1 has been reported to be cardioprotective (Das et al., 2012) and its absence is associated with cardiac hypertrophy (Cohen et al., 2003).
evidence: Citation to Cohen et al., 2003 provides established knowledge.

claim: Cav3 knockout mice show cardiomyopathy characterized by hypertrophy, heart dilation and reduced contractibility.
source: Cav3 knockout mice also show a cardiomyopathy characterized by hypertrophy, heart dilation and reduced contractibility (Woodman et al., 2002).
evidence: Citation to Woodman et al., 2002 provides established knowledge.

claim: Cav1 Cav3 double knockout animals develop cardiac hypertrophy and contractile failure.
source: Cav1 Cav3 double knockout animals, which completely lack caveolins because CAV2 is degraded in the absence of CAV1, develop cardiac hypertrophy and contractile failure (Park et al., 2002).
evidence: Citation to Park et al., 2002 provides established knowledge.

claim: Caveolar transport is required for the membrane translocation and correct function of fatty acid translocase FAT/CD36 in the healthy heart.
source: In the healthy heart, caveolar transport is required for the membrane translocation and correct function of fatty acid translocase FAT/CD36 (Ring et al., 2006; Son et al., 2018), which mediates the uptake of fatty acids.
evidence: Citations to Ring et al., 2006 and Son et al., 2018 provide established knowledge.

claim: Fatty acids are used by heart muscle cells to obtain about 50% to 70% of their energy.
source: Fatty acids will be delivered to the heart muscle cells that use them to obtain about 50% to 70% of their energy (Lopaschuk et al., 2010).
evidence: Citation to Lopaschuk et al., 2010 provides established knowledge.

claim: Absence of CD36 causes reduced fatty acids uptake and utilization by muscle cells.
source: Although CD36 is also expressed in the cardiomyocytes and its absence causes reduced fatty acids uptake and utilization by muscle cells (Coburn et al., 2000), it is endothelial CD36 that is critical for the uptake of fatty acids by the heart (Son et al., 2018).
evidence: Citations to Coburn et al., 2000 and Son et al., 2018 provide established knowledge.

claim: Endothelial CD36 is critical for the uptake of fatty acids by the heart.
source: Although CD36 is also expressed in the cardiomyocytes and its absence causes reduced fatty acids uptake and utilization by muscle cells (Coburn et al., 2000), it is endothelial CD36 that is critical for the uptake of fatty acids by the heart (Son et al., 2018).
evidence: Citation to Son et al., 2018 provides established knowledge.

claim: CD36 in the plasma membrane is critical for the function of the fatty acid translocase.
source: Accordingly, we found that CD36 in the plasma membrane, a localization that is critical for the function of the fatty acid translocase (Glatz and Luiken, 2018), is profoundly reduced in cultured ECs after knockdown of EPHB4 expression.
evidence: Citation to Glatz and Luiken, 2018 provides established knowledge; data in Figure 7D,E supports the observation.

claim: CD36-deficient mice have increased fatty acid uptake in the liver and develop fatty liver.
source: In line with the results described above, CD36-deficient mice have increased fatty acid uptake in the liver and develop fatty liver similar to Ephb4∆EC mutants (Goudriaan et al., 2003).
evidence: Citation to Goudriaan et al., 2003 provides established knowledge; comparison to Ephb4∆EC phenotype.

claim: Alterations in myocardial metabolic substrate have been related to heart failure and dilated cardiomyopathy.
source: Alterations in myocardial metabolic substrate have been related to heart failure and dilated cardiomyopathy (Neubauer et al., 1997) and it is noteworthy that DCM patients show CD36 deficiency (Tanaka et al., 1997).
evidence: Citations to Neubauer et al., 1997 and Tanaka et al., 1997 provide established knowledge.

claim: DCM patients show CD36 deficiency.
source: Alterations in myocardial metabolic substrate have been related to heart failure and dilated cardiomyopathy (Neubauer et al., 1997) and it is noteworthy that DCM patients show CD36 deficiency (Tanaka et al., 1997).
evidence: Citation to Tanaka et al., 1997 provides established knowledge.

claim: EphB4 signaling is required for maintaining the structural integrity of coronary capillaries.
source: Our findings also show that EphB4 signaling is required for maintaining the structural integrity of coronary capillaries.
evidence: Data from stretching assays, AFM, and TEM showing vascular ruptures support this claim.

claim: Caveolae-mediated trafficking is crucial for the turnover of focal adhesion points.
source: In this context, caveolae-mediated trafficking has been shown to be crucial for the turnover of focal adhesion points (Nethe and Hordijk, 2011).
evidence: Citation to Nethe and Hordijk, 2011 provides established knowledge.

claim: Proteins such as Vinculin or Paxillin form a molecular bridge which couples the cytoskeleton to membrane proteins such as integrins.
source: Proteins such as Vinculin or Paxillin form a molecular bridge, which couples the cytoskeleton to membrane proteins such as integrins (Burridge and Chrzanowska-Wodnicka, 1996; Ezzell et al., 1997) and thereby confers stiffness and mechanical stability to cells (Matthews et al., 2004).
evidence: Citations to Burridge and Chrzanowska-Wodnicka, 1996; Ezzell et al., 1997; and Matthews et al., 2004 provide established knowledge.

claim: The vasculature in the heart is exposed to constant mechanical stress due to heartbeat.
source: Mechanical stability is especially important in the heart, an organ where the vasculature is exposed to constant mechanical stress due to heartbeat (Thorin and Thorin-Trescases, 2009).
evidence: Citation to Thorin and Thorin-Trescases, 2009 provides established knowledge.

claim: EphB4 is required for the maintenance of focal adhesion points and thereby the structural integrity of ECs exposed to mechanical forces.
source: Our results suggest that EphB4, presumably due to its role in caveolar trafficking, is required for the maintenance of focal adhesion points and thereby the structural integrity of ECs exposed to mechanical forces.
evidence: Data from Figure 10A,C showing reduced Vinculin localization supports this inference.

claim: EphB4 and ephrin-B2 maintain fundamental properties of the endothelium in the adult heart.
source: Taking all together, we propose that EphB4 and its ligand ephrin-B2 maintain fundamental properties of the endothelium in the adult heart.
evidence: Summary inference based on all experimental data presented in the study.

claim: The function of EphB4 and ephrin-B2 in adult heart homeostasis is distinct from their well-established roles in angiogenic blood vessel growth.
source: This function is distinct from the well-established roles of these molecules in the regulation of angiogenic blood vessel growth (Adams et al., 1999; Gerety and Anderson, 2002; Gerety et al., 1999; Salvucci et al., 2006; Wang et al., 1998).
evidence: Citations to prior work on developmental roles; comparison to adult homeostasis functions.

claim: Eph/ephrin molecules, particularly ephrin-B2, are important regulators of intracellular trafficking processes such as receptor internalization.
source: Previous work has shown that Eph/ephrin molecules and, in particular, ephrin-B2 are important regulators of intracellular trafficking processes such as the internalization of receptors from the cell surface (Essmann et al., 2008; Gaitanos et al., 2016; Sawamiphak et al., 2010; Wang et al., 2010).
evidence: Citations to Essmann et al., 2008; Gaitanos et al., 2016; Sawamiphak et al., 2010; Wang et al., 2010 provide established knowledge.

claim: Eph/ephrin interactions may control fundamental processes such as endocytosis and vesicular trafficking in many cellular settings, while the local biological outcome depends on specific cargo molecules.
source: Thus, it is possible that Eph/ephrin interactions control fundamental processes, such as endocytosis and vesicular trafficking, in many different cellular settings, while the local biological outcome may strongly depend on the expression and function of specific cargo molecules.
evidence: Speculation based on known functions of Eph/ephrin molecules and observed tissue-specific effects.

claim: Defects in the coronary endothelium can result in defects resembling idiopathic cardiomyopathy.
source: Irrespective of the open questions outlined above, our work establishes that defects in the coronary endothelium can result in defects resembling idiopathic cardiomyopathy.
evidence: Summary inference based on the Ephb4∆EC phenotype resembling DCM.

claim: Mutations in the human EPHB4 gene are associated with Capillary Malformation-Arteriovenous Malformation 2.
source: Mutations in the human EPHB4 gene are associated with various pathologies, such Capillary Malformation-Arteriovenous Malformation 2 (Amyere et al., 2017) and vein of Galen aneurysmal malformations (Vivanti et al., 2018), which are known to be associated with heart failure.
evidence: Citation to Amyere et al., 2017 provides established knowledge.

claim: Mutations in the human EPHB4 gene are associated with vein of Galen aneurysmal malformations.
source: Mutations in the human EPHB4 gene are associated with various pathologies, such Capillary Malformation-Arteriovenous Malformation 2 (Amyere et al., 2017) and vein of Galen aneurysmal malformations (Vivanti et al., 2018), which are known to be associated with heart failure.
evidence: Citation to Vivanti et al., 2018 provides established knowledge.

claim: Vascular defects should be considered in the diagnosis and potentially treatment of cardiac disease in the future.
source: Accordingly, vascular defects should be considered in the diagnosis and, potentially, also treatment of cardiac disease in the future.
evidence: Speculation based on findings linking endothelial defects to cardiomyopathy-like phenotype.

claim: Dilated cardiomyopathy is the third most common cause of heart failure.
source: It is the third most common case of heart failure and the most frequent cause for heart transplantation (American Heart Association et al., 2006) with an estimated prevalence of 40 in 100.000 people (Manolio et al., 1992).
evidence: Citation to American Heart Association et al., 2006 provides established knowledge.

claim: Dilated cardiomyopathy is the most frequent cause for heart transplantation.
source: It is the third most common case of heart failure and the most frequent cause for heart transplantation (American Heart Association et al., 2006) with an estimated prevalence of 40 in 100.000 people (Manolio et al., 1992).
evidence: Citation to American Heart Association et al., 2006 provides established knowledge.

claim: The estimated prevalence of dilated cardiomyopathy is 40 in 100,000 people.
source: It is the third most common case of heart failure and the most frequent cause for heart transplantation (American Heart Association et al., 2006) with an estimated prevalence of 40 in 100.000 people (Manolio et al., 1992).
evidence: Citation to Manolio et al., 1992 provides established knowledge.

claim: Up to 80% of DCM patients present heart failure symptoms.
source: Up to 80% of DCM patients present heart failure symptoms (Dec and Fuster, 1994).
evidence: Citation to Dec and Fuster, 1994 provides established knowledge.

claim: The cellular ratio between cardiomyocytes and endothelial cells is 1:3.
source: The heart is a highly vascularized organ and capillaries reside in close proximity to almost every cardiomyocyte with a cellular ratio between cardiomyocytes and endothelial cells (ECs) of 1:3 (Brutsaert, 2003; Hsieh et al., 2006).
evidence: Citations to Brutsaert, 2003 and Hsieh et al., 2006 provide established knowledge.

claim: Around 35% of known DCM cases are due to mutations in genes that mainly encode myocardial cytoskeletal, sarcomeric and nuclear envelope proteins.
source: Around 35% of the known cases of DCM are due to mutations in genes that mainly encode myocardial cytoskeletal, sarcomeric and nuclear envelope proteins, but there are also acquired causes that include metabolic and endocrine disruptions (Garfinkel et al., 2018; Weintraub et al., 2017).
evidence: Citations to Garfinkel et al., 2018 and Weintraub et al., 2017 provide established knowledge.

claim: Most DCM cases are considered idiopathic, as the underlying cause is unknown.
source: Yet, most of the DCM cases are considered idiopathic, as the underlying cause is unknown (Towbin et al., 2006).
evidence: Citation to Towbin et al., 2006 provides established knowledge.

claim: Fatty acids are a crucial metabolic substrate for the heart.
source: Fatty acids are a crucial metabolic substrate for the heart (van der Vusse, 2000) and alterations in cardiomyocyte nutrient preference, such as enhanced glucose uptake and glycolysis, have been observed in multiple pathological conditions (Ritterhoff and Tian, 2017).
evidence: Citation to van der Vusse, 2000 provides established knowledge.

claim: Endothelial mutations in the laminin α4 subunit and integrin-linked kinase can cause cardiomyopathy.
source: Highlighting the importance of ECs in cardiac homeostasis, endothelial mutations in the laminin α4 subunit and integrin-linked kinase can cause cardiomyopathy (Knöll et al., 2007) and disruption of endothelial Notch signaling impairs fatty acid transport and leads to pathological heart remodeling (Jabs et al., 2018).
evidence: Citation to Knöll et al., 2007 provides established knowledge.

claim: Disruption of endothelial Notch signaling impairs fatty acid transport and leads to pathological heart remodeling.
source: Highlighting the importance of ECs in cardiac homeostasis, endothelial mutations in the laminin α4 subunit and integrin-linked kinase can cause cardiomyopathy (Knöll et al., 2007) and disruption of endothelial Notch signaling impairs fatty acid transport and leads to pathological heart remodeling (Jabs et al., 2018).
evidence: Citation to Jabs et al., 2018 provides established knowledge.

claim: EphB4 and ephrin-B2 regulate critical aspects of EC behavior in a cell-cell contact-dependent fashion.
source: The receptor tyrosine kinase EphB4 and its ligand, the transmembrane protein ephrin-B2, regulate critical aspects of EC behavior in a cell-cell contact-dependent fashion.
evidence: Established knowledge about Eph/ephrin signaling mechanisms.

claim: Signaling by ephrin-B2 and EphB4 has been implicated in the regulation of sprouting angiogenesis, vascular morphogenesis, and arteriovenous differentiation.
source: Signaling by ephrin-B2 and EphB4 has been implicated in the regulation of sprouting angiogenesis, vascular morphogenesis, arteriovenous differentiation (Pitulescu and Adams, 2010), and cancer (Pasquale, 2010), but little is known about the function of this ligand-receptor pair in adult organ homeostasis.
evidence: Citations to Pitulescu and Adams, 2010 and Pasquale, 2010 provide established knowledge.
